title: In the shop
summary: Near: deze (de-words and all plurals), dit (het-words in the singular). Far: die and dat in the same way. Dit is / dat zijn + noun never change. Die and dat also stand in for hij, zij, het, usually in first place.
explain:
`Deze`, `die`, `dit` and `dat` are the pointing words (*aanwijzende voornaamwoorden*): "this", "that", "these", "those". Which one you need depends on two things: is the thing near or far, and is the noun a de-word or a het-word? This is one of the reasons to learn every noun with its article.

### The four forms

| | near: this, these | far: that, those |
| de-word (de jas) | deze jas | die jas |
| het-word (het horloge) | dit horloge | dat horloge |
| every plural | deze jassen, deze horloges | die jassen, die horloges |

Every plural is a de-word, so the plural always takes `deze` or `die`: `dit horloge`, but `deze horloges`. A way to remember it: the forms that end in **t** go with he**t**.

> Deze trui is te groot. — This jumper is too big.
> Dat overhemd staat je goed. — That shirt suits you.
> Die laarzen zijn te duur. — Those boots are too expensive.

"Far" does not have to be far away. `Die` and `dat` are also used for something that was just mentioned, and in speech they are the most common choice. `Deze` and `dit` really point: this one here.

An adjective after these words always takes `-e` (unit A2 · 10): `dit mooie horloge`, `deze nieuwe schoenen`.

### On their own

All four can be used without a noun when it is clear what you mean. The form still follows the noun you have in mind. English adds "one", Dutch adds nothing.

> Ik neem deze. — I will take this one.
> Dit overhemd is te groot, maar dat past goed. — This shirt is too big, but that one fits well.

### Dit is …, dat zijn …

To introduce or identify a person or a thing, Dutch says `dit` or `dat` + `zijn` + noun. Here **dit and dat never change**: not for a de-word, not for a plural. Only the verb follows the noun: `is` for one, `zijn` for more.

> Dit is mijn broer. — This is my brother.
> Dat is de paskamer. — That is the fitting room.
> Dit zijn de nieuwe modellen. — These are the new models.
> Dat zijn mijn ouders. — Those are my parents.

Compare `Die schoenen zijn duur` (die + noun) with `Dat zijn dure schoenen` (dat + zijn + noun).

### Die and dat instead of hij, zij, het

In everyday speech Dutch very often says `die` or `dat` where English has "he", "she", "it", "they", "him" or "them", for people and things that were just mentioned. They usually stand first; when `die` or `dat` is not the subject, the subject comes after the verb.

> Ken je die verkoper? Nee, die ken ik niet. — Do you know that shop assistant? No, I do not know him.
> Waar zijn de sleutels? Die liggen op tafel. — Where are the keys? They are on the table.
> Hoe laat gaat de winkel dicht? Dat weet ik niet. — What time does the shop close? I do not know.

`Die` for de-words and plurals, `dat` for het-words. `Dat` also refers to a whole idea or sentence: `Dat weet ik niet`, `Dat is waar`, `Dat vind ik mooi`.

### Watch out

- A het-word takes `dit` and `dat` only in the singular: `dit product`, but `deze producten`, never *dit producten.
- To say who or what it is, always `dit` or `dat`: `Dit is mijn collega` (not *Deze is mijn collega), `Dat zijn mijn kinderen` (not *Die zijn mijn kinderen, and not *Dat is mijn kinderen).
- Without a noun after it, the pointing word follows the noun you mean: `Deze jas is duur en die is goedkoop`.
- "This one, that one": `Ik neem deze`, never *deze een.

`Die` and `dat` have two more jobs, which come later: `de man die daar staat` (unit B1 · 3) and `Ik weet dat hij komt` (unit A2 · 23).

### Compared with Ukrainian

Ukrainian chooses between `цей, ця, це, ці` and `той, та, те, ті` by gender, number and case. Dutch only looks at de or het and at near or far, and nothing changes after a preposition: `в цьому магазині` is simply `in deze winkel`. And `Це мій брат`, `Це мої батьки` work like `Dit is mijn broer`, `Dit zijn mijn ouders`: the pointing word stays the same. But Dutch must have the verb, and the verb shows the plural.

sentences.nl: Deze jas is te klein voor mij.
sentences.en: This coat is too small for me.
sentences.note: De jas is a de-word and the coat is right here, so deze. With a het-word it would be dit: dit overhemd.
alt: Deze jas is te klein voor me.

sentences.nl: Hoeveel kost dit horloge met korting?
sentences.en: How much does this watch cost with the discount?
sentences.note: Het horloge is a het-word in the singular and you have it in your hand: dit.
alt: Wat kost dit horloge met korting?

sentences.nl: Deze horloges zijn in de aanbieding.
sentences.note: The plural always takes deze (or die), also for a het-word: dit horloge, but deze horloges.

sentences.nl: Ik wil die zwarte schoenen graag passen.
sentences.en: I would like to try on those black shoes.
sentences.note: Schoenen is plural and the shoes are further away: die. The adjective after die takes -e: zwarte.
alt: Ik wil graag die zwarte schoenen passen.

sentences.nl: Wij verkopen dat product niet meer.
sentences.en: We no longer sell that product.
sentences.note: Het product is a het-word in the singular, and it is not here in front of us: dat. In the plural it would be die producten.
alt: We verkopen dat product niet meer.
Dat product verkopen wij niet meer.
Dat product verkopen we niet meer.

sentences.nl: Welke maat wilt u, deze of die?
sentences.en: Which size would you (formal) like, this one or that one?
sentences.note: Deze and die stand on their own here: the noun maat is not repeated. De maat is a de-word, so deze and die, not dit and dat. Dutch has no word for 'one'.
alt: Welke maat wil u, deze of die?

sentences.en: This is the new shop assistant.
sentences.note: To introduce someone Dutch uses dit is, also for a de-word like de verkoper. Deze is … would be wrong here.

sentences.nl: Dat zijn de prijzen van vorig jaar.
sentences.note: Dat stays dat, also before a plural. Only the verb changes: zijn, because de prijzen is plural.

sentences.nl: Waar is de bon? Die heb ik niet meer.
sentences.en: Where is the receipt? I do not have it any more. (it: die, in first place)
sentences.note: Die stands for de bon, a de-word, and comes first, so the verb heb follows and then the subject ik. With hem it would be: Ik heb hem niet meer.

sentences.nl: Dat vind ik een goede prijs.
sentences.en: I think that is a good price.
sentences.note: Dat refers to what was just said or shown, not to a noun. It stands first, so the verb vind comes before ik.
alt: Ik vind dat een goede prijs.

exercises.en: This discount is only valid today.
exercises.note: Korting is a de-word, like all words in -ing, so deze. Dit and dat only go with het-words in the singular.

exercises.en: What do you think of this brand?
exercises.note: Het merk is a het-word in the singular: dit. Deze and die go with de-words and with plurals.
To say what something is, Dutch uses dit or dat before zijn, also when the noun is plural. Only the verb shows the plural: dit zijn.

exercises.nl: Deze jas kost honderd euro en ___ kost vijftig euro.
exercises.en: This coat costs a hundred euros and that one costs fifty euros.
exercises.note: Die stands on its own here and still means a jas, a de-word: die. Nothing is added for English 'one'.

exercises.nl: Waar is de klant? ___ staat bij de kassa.
exercises.en: Where is the customer? She is standing at the checkout.
exercises.note: In speech die often replaces hij or zij. De klant is a de-word, so die. Dat would be for a het-word.

exercises.en: I would like to exchange this shirt.
exercises.note: Het overhemd is a het-word in the singular, and you are holding it: dit.
De paskamer is a de-word, and it is over there: die.
Dit does not change, but the verb follows the noun after it. Producten is plural, so zijn.

exercises.nl: Kan ik hier pinnen? Ja, ___ (that) kan.
exercises.en: Can I pay by card here? Yes, you can.
exercises.note: Dat refers to the whole idea of paying by card, not to a noun. For an idea or a whole sentence it is always dat.

answers: Die schoenen breng ik morgen terug.
exercises.en: I am taking those shoes back tomorrow.
exercises.note: Die schoenen is the object and stands first, so the verb comes second and ik after it. The prefix of terugbrengen goes to the end.
Every plural takes deze, also the plural of a het-word. The verb becomes plural too: zijn.
Rek is a het-word, so in the singular deze becomes dit. The verb becomes singular too: is.

exercises.task: Point at things further away: change this to that, twice.
exercises.from: Deze klant wil dit horloge ruilen.
answers: Die klant wil dat horloge ruilen.
exercises.en: That customer wants to exchange that watch.
exercises.note: Deze becomes die (de klant) and dit becomes dat (het horloge). The pairs are deze / die and dit / dat.

exercises.task: Say the same with Dat zijn …
exercises.note: Before zijn + noun it is dat, also for a plural. The adjective now stands before the noun and takes -e: dure.
Schoenen is plural, and a plural never takes dit or dat. Near is deze. Die would also be a correct sentence, for shoes that are further away.
To introduce a person Dutch uses dit is (or dat is), whether the noun is a de-word or a het-word. Deze is … is only right without a noun after it: Deze is van mij.
